summary: A 100-foot Aermotor lookout from 1950 on Beaver Mountain in Oklahoma's Cookson Hills, reported surplus and possibly moved to Sand Springs; its current location is unconfirmed.

facts.design: 100-foot Aermotor tower with a metal 7 by 7 foot cab
facts.status_note: A News On 6 report called the lookout abandoned and surplus, and a Sand Springs news item says the city bought it for a move. No source confirms the move, so its current location is unconfirmed.

access.note: Summit reached by roads that may be gated; access depends on gate openings, wildlife area operations and controlled hunts. Not confirmed open for climbing.

visit.trail_note: Summit reached by road or road hike; access depends on gates and controlled hunts

events.note: 100-foot Aermotor tower with a 7x7 steel cab erected on the Cookson Hills Wildlife Management Area
Manned by ranger Jess Morton, per a 1960 Stilwell Democrat-Journal report
Registered November 7, 1997 as US 240, OK 3; nominated by Patrick McDowell, Oklahoma Forestry Services

evidence.supports: Aermotor tower, 100 feet, metal 7 by 7 foot cab, in the Cookson Hills WMA in northeast Oklahoma
evidence.quote: Located in the Cookson Hills Wildlife Management Area in Northeast Oklahoma, Beaver Fire Tower is a 100’ Aermotor tower with metal 7’ x 7’ cab.
Constructed in 1950, it remained in active service until 1997.

evidence.supports: erected in 1950 as a 100-foot Aermotor tower with a 7x7 steel cab
evidence.quote: 1950: A 100-foot Aermotor tower with a 7x7 steel cab was erected on the Cookson Hills Wildlife Management Area.

evidence.supports: February 25, 1960 report of ranger Jess Morton manning the tower, able to signal on sighting trespassers or fire
evidence.quote: A hundred-foot lookout tower on Beaver mountain manned by Jess Morton, the ranger, can signal on sight of trespassers or a trace of fire.

evidence.supports: roofed hollow stump serves as visitor registration site; the register does not place it near the summit
evidence.quote: A unique roofed hollow stump (large enough to hold four people) serves as a visitor registration site.

evidence.supports: nominated by Patrick McDowell of Oklahoma Forestry Services
evidence.quote:
Nominated by
Patrick McDowell, Oklahoma Forestry Services

evidence.supports: 100-foot Aermotor tower constructed in 1950, officially used until 1997
evidence.quote: The top of the mountain is most notably known for its fire lookout, a 100' tall Aermotor tower constructed during 1950 and officially used until 1997.

evidence.supports: Beaver Mountain is the highest point in Cherokee County
evidence.quote: Beaver Mountain is the highest point of Cherokee County, Oklahoma.

evidence.supports: summit access depends on gate openings, WMA operations and controlled hunts
evidence.quote: Beaver Mountain is accessible via roads but type access depends upon current gate openings, Cookson WMA operations, and active controlled hunts.

evidence.supports: Forestry Service no longer needs most fire towers; this one considered surplus
evidence.quote: The Oklahoma Forestry Service no longer needs most fire towers, so one in Cherokee County, even though it’s historic, is considered surplus.

evidence.supports: lookout abandoned, could move to Keystone Ancient Forest Preserve in Sand Springs
evidence.quote: The Beaver Mountain Lookout was used to protect the forest near Cookson from the 1950’s to 1997, and now abandoned, it could moved to the Keystone Ancient Forest Preserve in Sand Springs.

evidence.supports: tower 100 feet tall and still sound
evidence.quote: It’s 100 feet to the top of the old tower, which despite its age, is still sound.

evidence.supports: Sand Springs city recently purchased a 100-foot lookout tower for the forest
evidence.quote: Also in the works for the forest is a 100-foot fire lookout tower that the City recently purchased.
The disused tower was acquired at a cost of $108,000 from Cookson, Oklahoma.

evidence.supports: tower listed on the National Historic Lookout Register
evidence.quote: It is listed on the National Historic Lookout Register and will give visitors the opportunity to see from above the forest canopy.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record lists the tower as standing. The 2019 News On 6 report and the later Sand Springs item describe it as surplus and bought for a move, so the record may be out of date, though the move is not confirmed.

sources.title: Oklahoma Forestry Service Possibly Moving Cherokee Co. Tower
Sand Springs breaks ground on new Keystone Ancient Forest Visitor Center

notes_for_editor: The tower's location after the city's purchase is unconfirmed. The Sandite Pride item does not name the tower but its details match Beaver's (100 feet, from Cookson, on the register); a human should check this with Sand Springs Parks or the Oklahoma Forestry Services. The News On 6 story is dated October 8, 2019 on the cached page. The register does not place the stump near the summit, so the story omits that detail. The Sandite Pride item's date is not printed; its URL suggests March 2020. Because the date and move are uncertain, no event was recorded for either. The record's status 'standing' may be out of date. The 1960 staffing comes from one newspaper quote. Height 30.5 m is the NHLR's 100 feet. The SummitPost access note is undated.
